name.text: Calculating coordinates of a point on a unit circle.

questiontext.text:
Let \(P\) be the point where the terminal side of the angle \(\theta = {@theta@}\) meets the unit circle. The angle is measured anticlockwise from the positive \(x\)-axis, and the unit circle has centre \(O(0,\,0)\) and radius \(1\). The diagram shows the angle \(\theta\) and the point \(P\).

[[jsxgraph width="320px" height="320px"]] (function() { var th = {#float(theta)#}; var px = Math.cos(th), py = Math.sin(th); var b = JXG.JSXGraph.initBoard(divid, {boundingbox:[-1.45, 1.45, 1.45, -1.45], axis:false, grid:false, keepaspectratio:true, showNavigation:false, showCopyright:false}); b.create('arrow', [[-1.35, 0], [1.35, 0]], {strokeColor:'#444', fixed:true, highlight:false}); b.create('arrow', [[0, -1.35], [0, 1.35]], {strokeColor:'#444', fixed:true, highlight:false}); b.create('text', [1.3, -0.13, 'x'], {fixed:true}); b.create('text', [-0.15, 1.3, 'y'], {fixed:true}); b.create('text', [1.03, -0.12, '1'], {fixed:true}); b.create('text', [-1.22, -0.12, '\u22121'], {fixed:true}); b.create('text', [0.05, 1.09, '1'], {fixed:true}); b.create('text', [0.05, -1.1, '\u22121'], {fixed:true}); var O = b.create('point', [0, 0], {name:'O', fixed:true, size:2, color:'#222', label:{offset:[-14,-12]}}); b.create('circle', [O, 1], {strokeColor:'#1565c0', strokeWidth:2, fixed:true, highlight:false}); var A = b.create('point', [1, 0], {visible:false, fixed:true}); var P = b.create('point', [px, py], {name:'P', fixed:true, size:4, color:'#c62828', label:{offset:[px > 0 ? 10 : -22, py > 0 ? 14 : -16]}}); b.create('segment', [O, P], {strokeColor:'#c62828', strokeWidth:2, fixed:true}); b.create('angle', [A, O, P], {radius:0.25, name:'\u03b8', fillColor:'#ffb74d', strokeColor:'#ef6c00', fillOpacity:0.35, fixed:true}); })(); [[/jsxgraph]]

Find the exact coordinates \((x,\,y)\) of the point \(P\).

Type your answer as \([x, y]\) using exact values, for example [-sqrt(3)/2, 1/2]. Do not use decimals, and do not use sin or cos in your answer.

\(P = \) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution

The idea. For any angle \(\theta\), the point where its terminal side meets the unit circle is \(P = (\cos\theta,\, \sin\theta)\). The radius is \(1\), so the \(x\)-coordinate of \(P\) is \(\cos\theta\) and the \(y\)-coordinate is \(\sin\theta\). To find them exactly, we use the reference angle for the size of each coordinate and the quadrant for its sign.

Step 1: find the quadrant. \(\theta = {@theta@}\) (that is, \({@thetadeg@}^\circ\)) lies in Quadrant {@quadname@}[[if test="is(quad=1)"]], between \(0\) and \(\frac{\pi}{2}\)[[/if]][[if test="is(quad=2)"]], between \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\pi\)[[/if]][[if test="is(quad=3)"]], between \(\pi\) and \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\)[[/if]][[if test="is(quad=4)"]], between \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\) and \(2\pi\)[[/if]].

Step 2: find the reference angle \(\alpha\). The reference angle is the acute angle between the terminal side and the \(x\)-axis. [[if test="is(quad=1)"]]In Quadrant I the angle is already acute, so \(\alpha = \theta = {@refang@}\).[[/if]] [[if test="is(quad=2)"]]In Quadrant II, \(\alpha = \pi - \theta = \pi - {@theta@} = {@refang@}\).[[/if]] [[if test="is(quad=3)"]]In Quadrant III, \(\alpha = \theta - \pi = {@theta@} - \pi = {@refang@}\).[[/if]] [[if test="is(quad=4)"]]In Quadrant IV, \(\alpha = 2\pi - \theta = 2\pi - {@theta@} = {@refang@}\).[[/if]]

Step 3: use the exact values for the reference angle. From the special triangles,

\[ \cos {@refang@} = {@abs(x0)@}, \qquad \sin {@refang@} = {@abs(y0)@}. \]

These are the sizes of the coordinates of \(P\), without their signs.

Step 4: decide the signs from the quadrant. In Quadrant {@quadname@}, \(P\) is [[if test="is(x0>0)"]]to the right of the \(y\)-axis, so \(x\) is positive,[[else]]to the left of the \(y\)-axis, so \(x\) is negative,[[/if]] and [[if test="is(y0>0)"]]above the \(x\)-axis, so \(y\) is positive.[[else]]below the \(x\)-axis, so \(y\) is negative.[[/if]] Therefore

\[ x = \cos {@theta@} = {@x0@}, \qquad y = \sin {@theta@} = {@y0@}. \]

Step 5: write down the coordinates.

\[ P = \left( {@x0@},\, {@y0@} \right). \]

The diagram shows \(\theta\) in orange[[if test="is(quad>1)"]] and the reference angle \(\alpha\) in green[[/if]]. The dashed line drops from \(P\) to the \(x\)-axis, showing \(y\) as the height of \(P\) and \(x\) as its distance across from \(O\).

[[jsxgraph width="360px" height="360px"]] (function() { var th = {#float(theta)#}, q = {#quad#}; var px = Math.cos(th), py = Math.sin(th); var b = JXG.JSXGraph.initBoard(divid, {boundingbox:[-1.5, 1.5, 1.5, -1.5], axis:true, grid:false, keepaspectratio:true, showNavigation:false, showCopyright:false}); var O = b.create('point', [0, 0], {name:'O', fixed:true, size:2, color:'#222', label:{offset:[-14,-12]}}); b.create('circle', [O, 1], {strokeColor:'#1565c0', strokeWidth:2, fixed:true, highlight:false}); var A = b.create('point', [1, 0], {visible:false, fixed:true}); var Am = b.create('point', [-1, 0], {visible:false, fixed:true}); var P = b.create('point', [px, py], {name:'P', fixed:true, size:4, color:'#c62828', label:{offset:[px > 0 ? 10 : -22, py > 0 ? 14 : -16]}}); b.create('segment', [O, P], {strokeColor:'#c62828', strokeWidth:2, fixed:true}); var Fp = b.create('point', [px, 0], {visible:false, fixed:true}); b.create('segment', [P, Fp], {dash:2, strokeColor:'#888', fixed:true}); b.create('angle', [A, O, P], {radius:0.22, name:'θ', fillColor:'#ffb74d', strokeColor:'#ef6c00', fillOpacity:0.35, fixed:true}); var refStyle = {radius:0.45, name:'α', fillColor:'#81c784', strokeColor:'#2e7d32', fillOpacity:0.35, fixed:true}; if (q == 2) { b.create('angle', [P, O, Am], refStyle); } if (q == 3) { b.create('angle', [Am, O, P], refStyle); } if (q == 4) { b.create('angle', [P, O, A], refStyle); } })(); [[/jsxgraph]]

Trigonometric ratios. Reading the coordinates of \(P\) gives the ratios of \(\theta\) directly: \(\cos {@theta@} = {@x0@}\), \(\sin {@theta@} = {@y0@}\), and \(\tan {@theta@} = \dfrac{y}{x} = {@tanv@}\).

prtcorrect.text: Correct answer, well done.

prtpartiallycorrect.text: Your answer is partially correct.

prtincorrect.text: Incorrect answer.

truefeedback.text: Your \(y\)-coordinate is right, but your \(x\)-coordinate has the wrong sign. In which quadrant does \(\theta = {@theta@}\) lie? Is \(P\) to the left or to the right of the \(y\)-axis there?
Your \(x\)-coordinate is right, but your \(y\)-coordinate has the wrong sign. In which quadrant does \(\theta = {@theta@}\) lie? Is \(P\) above or below the \(x\)-axis there?
Both of your signs are wrong, so your point is in the quadrant opposite to \(P\). Find the quadrant of \(\theta = {@theta@}\) first, then use it to decide the sign of each coordinate.
It looks as if you have swapped the coordinates. On the unit circle the \(x\)-coordinate is \(\cos\theta\) and the \(y\)-coordinate is \(\sin\theta\).

node.description: Right signs, cos and sin of the reference angle swapped

truefeedback.text: Your signs are right, but the sizes of the coordinates are the wrong way round. Find the reference angle, then check which of its cosine and sine is the larger.

falsefeedback.text: Find the reference angle (the acute angle between the terminal side and the \(x\)-axis) and use its exact cosine and sine. Then use the quadrant of \(\theta\) to decide the sign of each coordinate. Remember that \(x = \cos\theta\) and \(y = \sin\theta\).
